tasks.task_text:
Summary

`omh memory dream` is documented as a pure report — the subcommand help says *"Report whether memory consolidation is due, and why. Never consolidates."* and `cmd_memory_dream` returns `{"evaluated": false}` with no `due` key when `--evaluate` is absent.

It is not a pure report. Running it raises a consolidation brief, writes it to disk, and **marks its reasons as already fired**, which suppresses the next real brief for every standing condition that has not changed.

Reproduction

Self-contained; no dependency on the operator's real `~/.hermes`.

```sh
ROOT=$(mktemp -d); mkdir -p "$ROOT/.hermes/memories" "$ROOT/.omh"
python3 -c "import pathlib; pathlib.Path('$ROOT/.hermes/memories/MEMORY.md').write_text('- ' + 'x'*2100 + '\n')"
B=(uv run python -m omh.cli --omh-home "$ROOT/.omh" --hermes-home "$ROOT/.hermes")

ls "$ROOT/.omh/memory" 2>/dev/null || echo "no memory dir yet"

"${B[@]}" memory dream            # documented: report only, never consolidates
ls "$ROOT/.omh/memory"
cat "$ROOT/.omh/memory/dreaming.json"

"${B[@]}" memory dream --evaluate # the standing condition is unchanged and still true
```

Observed:

```
=== 1. brief present before any command? ===
no
=== 2. run: omh memory dream   (docs: 'Report ... Never consolidates') ===
  evaluated = False  due key present = False
=== 3. brief written to disk by that read-only report? ===
  consolidation.json  YES
  dreaming.json       YES
  last_reasons = ['headroom_below_floor:98<=300']
=== 4. the standing condition is unchanged and still true; ask properly ===
  due = False  reasons = []
```

Step 4 is the damage. The Hermes memory file is still 98 characters from its cap, but the scheduler now reports nothing is due, because step 2 already recorded that reason as fired.

Environment

macOS 25.5.0, Python 3.11 via `uv`, repo at `9c134895` + main.

tasks.task_text:
Summary

`_memory_tokens` in `src/workflows/memory.py` requires ASCII tokens to be at least 3 characters:

```python
_MEMORY_ASCII_TOKEN = re.compile(r"[a-z0-9_/-]{3,}")
```

Two-letter technical terms are therefore never indexed and never queryable: `CI`, `DB`, `UI`, `UX`, `QA`, `AI`, `ML`, `PR`, `JS`, `TS`, `VM`, `S3`, `go`. Because the zero-token fallback and the zero-overlap path take **opposite** branches, the same store answers the same subject with either everything or nothing depending on how many words the operator typed.

Reproduction

Three approved records:

| summary | tags |
| --- | --- |
| `CI runs on GitHub Actions for every push` | `ci` |
| `Postgres is the primary DB for the api service` | `db` |
| `Terraform provisions the staging cluster` | `infra` |

```
  query='CI'                   included=3  excluded=[]
  query='ci failures'          included=0  excluded=[(mem_1b01ec53,'no_query_overlap'),
                                                     (mem_75d9b039,'no_query_overlap'),
                                                     (mem_de8ac37b,'no_query_overlap')]
  query='which DB do we use'   included=0
  query='terraform'            included=1  ['Terraform provisions the staging cluster']
```

- `CI` tokenizes to `∅`, so `_memory_recall_score` returns its "no indexable tokens" fallback of `1` for every record. The pack hands the executor Postgres and Terraform as CI context, with `excluded=[]` — no signal at all that the query was never actually matched.
- `ci failures` tokenizes to `{failures}`. Every record is excluded as `no_query_overlap`, **including the one whose summary begins with the query word and carries `ci` as a tag**. The most natural phrasing an operator would type returns zero results.
- Tag matching cannot rescue it. `tag_overlap = query_tokens & set(tags)` is computed from the same dropped token set, so a 2-character tag is unmatchable by construction: `_memory_recall_score(rec, "ci") == 1` (the fallback), never `5 + 10`.

Environment

macOS 25.5.0, Python 3.11 via `uv`, main at `9c134895`.
tasks.title: fix: let recall reach two-letter technical terms (CI, DB, UI, QA)

tasks.task_text:
Summary

An approved memory record carries its expiry deadline **twice**: `record["ttl"]["expires_at"]` and `record["retention"]["expires_at"]`. Different surfaces read different copies, and nothing keeps them equal.

- recall exclusion, `memory retire`, `memory status`, and the dreaming record-expiry counts read `ttl.expires_at`, via `classify_record_expiry` → `classify_record_expiry_v1_compat`.
- the lifecycle plans (`memory prune`, `memory restore`, the standard-retirement guard) read `retention.expires_at`, via `_expiry_reason` in `src/workflows/_memory_lifecycle_plans.py`.

`classify_record_expiry` documents itself as the global invariant:

> The single source of truth for what "expired" means. Recall exclusion and retirement both route through this so they can never disagree.

The lifecycle half does not route through it, so they can disagree — and there is no test asserting the two fields stay equal.

Reproduction

One record, one moment, two verdicts:

```
=== one record, one moment, two verdicts ===
  backdate ttl.expires_at only       retire says expired=1   prune says prune_requires_expired_approved_volatile
  backdate retention.expires_at only retire says expired=0   prune says planned
  backdate both (consistent)         retire says expired=1   prune says planned
```

Script (`repro_two_clocks.sh`): capture an `--ttl-days 1 --retention-class volatile` record, approve it, edit exactly one of the two `expires_at` fields to a past date, then ask both surfaces.

Row 1 is what an operator hits: `omh memory retire` reports the record as expired, and `omh memory prune <id> --revision 1` refuses it with `prune_requires_expired_approved_volatile` — the reason code asserts the record is not expired, in the same store, in the same second.

Row 2 is the inverse and the more dangerous one: the record is still delivered by recall as fresh while `prune` is willing to plan a hard delete of it.

Environment

macOS 25.5.0, Python 3.11 via `uv`, main at `9c134895`.
tasks.title: fix: give one record one expiry deadline across every surface

tasks.task_text:
What breaks

On the Hermes-native delegation lane, a genuinely-recorded `$0.00` from the host is indistinguishable from "the host recorded nothing", and gets silently replaced by an approximation.

`src/plugin_bundle/omh/hermes_delegation.py`:

```python
cost = usage.get("actual_cost_usd") or usage.get("estimated_cost_usd")
cost_approximate = False
if not cost:
    approx = _approximate_cost_usd(child["model"], input_tokens, output_tokens, cache_read)
    if approx is not None:
        cost = approx
        cost_approximate = True
```

`0.0` is falsy, so a real subscription-tier zero takes the same branch as a missing value. A free run is then reported as a priced one.

And when the model is *also* absent from the price table, `_approximate_cost_usd` returns `None`, the row keeps `cost_usd: 0.0` with **no** `cost_approximate` flag, and renders identically to a genuine free run — the HUD's `> 0` gate hides it either way, so the operator cannot tell the difference in either direction.
tasks.title: fix(cost): an unpriceable unrecorded cost is unknown, not free

tasks.task_text:
Why This Exists

#1351 stopped the workspace boundary from depending on a file extension. Its reviewer then reported that a token gluing a path to a delimiter is declared verbatim, and that percent-encoded traversals are declared but never decoded — non-blocking at the time because neither traverses as a literal filesystem name. Probing those two turned up a third, sharper one. Every input below reached an allowed, dispatchable handoff on `main`:

```
fix x;../outside/marker.txt        declared ['x;../outside/marker.txt']   allow
fix a=b=../outside/marker.txt      declared ['b=../outside/marker.txt']   allow
fix a/b:../outside/marker.txt                                            allow
fix"../outside/marker.txt"                                               allow
fix x;..\outside\marker.txt                                              allow
fix ..%2foutside/marker.txt                                              allow
fix %2e%2e%2foutside%2fmarker.txt                                        allow
fix %2fetc%2fmarker.txt                                                  allow
fix ../outside/marker.py?v=1       declared NOTHING                      allow
```

One mechanism underneath all of them: extraction produced exactly one spelling per token, and containment reads segments. `_path_parts` (`src/quality/safety_preflight.py`) splits on `/` and `\` only, so a `..` glued to a delimiter is not a segment it can see, and a `..` spelled `%2e%2e` is not one either. The last line is the worst of them: the assignment right-hand-side rewrite discarded an already-anchored path and declared its query value instead, so naming an escaping file with a query string declared no target at all.
tasks.title: fix(coding): declare the glued and encoded spellings a target token hides

tasks.task_text:
Why This Exists

#1353 shipped with two residuals written into a comment at the decoding site:

1. **Single-pass decoding.** `fix %252e%252e/outside/marker.txt` decoded once to `%2e%2e/outside/marker.txt`, stopped, was declared as a literal filename, and **allowed**.
2. **The halved allowance.** Every decoded spelling was declared beside its original, so a message naming ordinary `%20` filenames burned two slots each and denied on count at roughly half of `MAX_TARGET_PATHS`.
tasks.title: fix(coding): decode to a fixpoint, and charge a slot only when containment would read it

Why This Exists

- A user updating 2.0.0 → 2.0.1 on an installer-managed machine reported `OMH update stopped during post_activation; the known-good generation remains active.` with nothing else to act on.
- The staged transaction renders the candidate pack into a new generation directory, then re-enters the update against the real home. That home's `manifest.json` still describes the active generation's pack, so the installer compared the candidate's fresh render against the recorded hashes and reported every skill the catalog had changed since the last install as a "local modification", refused without `--force`, and the transaction rolled back.
- A machine whose recorded pack already matched the candidate render passed, which is why it did not reproduce locally. Every real version bump through the staged path would have hit it.
tasks.title: fix(update): staged re-entry judges the candidate pack by its own manifest

tasks.task_text:
Motivation

Owner report: `omh update` printed `Previous release: 2.0.2 / Installed release: 2.0.1 / Release version: 2.0.2 -> 2.0.1`. Reconstructed on the owner machine:

- The update was run from inside the source checkout, which ships a top-level `omh/` shim package (`omh/__init__.py` re-pointing at `src/`). The checkout was 74 commits behind main, at version 2.0.1.
- `python -m omh.cli` puts the working directory at `sys.path[0]`, so every re-entry imported the checkout's stale code instead of the generation venv's 2.0.2 package. Verified: the same venv python reports `omh 2.0.1` from the checkout cwd and `omh 2.0.2` from `/tmp`; with `-P` it reports 2.0.2 from the checkout.
- The stale 2.0.1 installer (pre-#1377) judged the fresh candidate against the home manifest, refused, and the transaction rolled back to the 2.0.2 generation. The rollback re-entry, also running checkout code, printed the card and stamped `~/.omh/manifest.json` with `"version": "2.0.1"`. The active generation remained 2.0.2 throughout (`omh --version` says 2.0.2); only the manifest and the card were wrong.
tasks.title: fix(update): spawned interpreters run the generation's package, not the cwd's

tasks.task_text:
Why This Exists

Persistent memory is context every later turn pays for, which is what makes it useful and why it should not hold conversation archaeology. The assessment found OMH already does the expensive half well: per-turn injection is bounded by four independent caps (system blocks 6000 chars; records 2400 chars / 6 records / 500-char summaries; consolidation brief 1600 chars / 6 items; references by label index only) with overflow reported as `render_budget_exhausted` rather than silently dropped; nothing writes without an explicit act; the Hermes write hook journals shape and never text; retention classes already age `episode` records out. What was missing was the routing advice at the moment of capture, and a docstring that promised more than its patterns delivered.
tasks.title: feat(memory): route past-session history to the session store, not a record

tasks.task_text:
Summary

`omh chat route-hint` — and therefore the message-specific `[OMH Route Hint]` rail rendered by the
Hermes plugin — reports `no_hint` for messages that match only a **user** trigger language pack,
while `omh recommend` and the *same payload's own* `route_decision` resolve the identical message to
the right skill with `confidence=high`. Adding a language through the documented user-pack mechanism
(`<omh-home>/routing/trigger-packs/<lang>.json`) upgrades scoring/recommendation but leaves the
hint-card surface silent — and the hint card is the surface a chat user actually sees.

Reproduction

```bash
mkdir -p /tmp/omh-repro/routing/trigger-packs
cat > /tmp/omh-repro/routing/trigger-packs/es.json <<'EOF'
{
  "schema_version": "trigger_language_pack/v1",
  "language": "es",
  "skills": { "code-review": ["hacer una revision de codigo"] }
}
EOF
export OMH_HOME=/tmp/omh-repro

# scoring layer: sees the user pack
omh recommend "hacer una revision de codigo" --limit 1

# hint card layer: same message, same process environment
omh chat route-hint "hacer una revision de codigo"
omh chat route-hint "hacer una revision de codigo" --json

# control: a phrase that IS in a shipped cue list
omh chat route-hint "do a code review"
```

`omh doctor` confirms the pack is loaded (on the machine where this was reproduced with `ru`):
`trigger language packs shipped: ja (84 phrases), ko (949 phrases), zh (81 phrases); user packs: ru (226 phrases)`.

Observed evidence

```text
$ omh recommend "hacer una revision de codigo" --limit 1
OMH recommendation
1. code-review [high]
   Why: Matched workflow trigger language for this task.

$ omh chat route-hint "hacer una revision de codigo"
Status: no_hint
Workflow: none
Hints: 0
[omh] no strong workflow hint yet.

$ omh chat route-hint "hacer una revision de codigo" --json   # key fields
route_hint.status      : no_hint
route_decision         : {action: dispatch, confidence: high, router_stage: recommendation,
                          selected_skill: code-review}

$ omh chat route-hint "do a code review"                       # control
Status: hinted
Workflow: ulw-work
Matched cues: code review, review
```

Note the internal contradiction in one payload: `route_decision.selected_skill = code-review`
(`confidence=high`, `router_stage=recommendation`) while `route_hint.status = no_hint`.

Observed in Hermes chat as well: with a user pack installed, first-turn messages in the packed
language produce no plugin `[OMH Route Hint]` block in the turn, while `omh recommend` returns
high-confidence workflows for the same text. In that deployment hints had to be injected externally
(a Hermes `pre_llm_call` shell hook calling `omh recommend`), which is a workaround, not the
designed rail.

Environment

- OMH 2.0.3, installed package (`omh doctor`: "build identity unavailable: installed package"),
  Python 3.14 venv under the OMH generation dir.
- Hermes Agent, Linux (CachyOS); profile-scoped install (`omh setup`, user scope).
- Reproduced with both `es` (1 phrase, shown above) and `ru` (226 phrases) user packs; the
  mechanism is language-agnostic.
- `omh doctor`: 44/44 passing with the user pack installed.
tasks.title: fix(routing): the route hint honours user trigger language packs
